pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11 (META; the domain's most-connected node). How scientific knowledge CHANGES — that our picture of dinosaurs has been repeatedly revised as new evidence arrives — taught through real reversals so children see science as self-correcting, evidence-led and provisional, not a fixed set of facts.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 working-scientifically (using evidence to answer questions; recognising that scientific ideas change) and Y6 Evolution as the content vehicle.
• Standards — US (NGSS): Nature of Science — 'scientific knowledge is open to revision in light of new evidence' and 'science is a human endeavour'.
• Operational details: use concrete reversals — sluggish, scaly, tail-dragging dinosaurs → active, often feathered, tail-up animals; Brontosaurus/Apatosaurus saga; warm- vs cold-blooded debate. Show different scientists can read the SAME evidence differently, and the best-supported explanation fits the MOST evidence from multiple independent sources. Stress that changing your mind on new evidence is a STRENGTH, not a failure.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (concrete, ~9): give one thing scientists used to think about dinosaurs and what they think now. Tier B (transitional, ~10): explain WHAT NEW EVIDENCE (e.g. feathered fossils) changed the picture. Tier C (formal, ~11): explain why scientists changing their minds is a strength, and how competing ideas are judged by weight of evidence.
bestPractices: Teach through concrete, documented reversals (feathered dinosaurs, Brontosaurus) rather than abstract statements about 'science changing'.
Always pair a changed idea with the EVIDENCE that changed it, so revision looks reasoned, not arbitrary.
Frame mind-changing as a strength of science, countering the idea that changing conclusions means scientists were 'wrong' or unreliable.
Show competing interpretations of the same evidence to normalise disagreement resolved by weight of evidence.
Connect to the child's own reasoning — invite predictions, then update them with evidence, mirroring the scientific process.
keyRepresentations: Then-vs-now dinosaur reconstructions with the evidence that drove each change.
A timeline of a single idea (e.g. dinosaur metabolism) being revised.
A feathered-theropod fossil slab as a pivotal piece of new evidence.
A 'best current picture' label emphasising provisional, updatable knowledge.
commonMisconceptions: 'Science is a fixed set of facts that don't change' — knowledge is revised as evidence improves.
'If scientists change their minds, they were wrong / science is unreliable' — revision on evidence is how science works and is a strength.
'Whatever is in the textbook is final truth' — it is the best current explanation, open to revision.
'Scientists just have opinions' — conclusions are constrained by and judged on evidence.
'A single new discovery instantly overturns everything' — change usually reflects accumulating evidence from multiple sources.

learn.summary: Teaches a nature-of-science idea for ages 9–11: scientific knowledge about dinosaurs has been repeatedly revised as new evidence arrived, so science is evidence-led, self-correcting and provisional rather than a fixed set of facts. Learners examine documented reversals (sluggish scaly tail-draggers to active, often feathered, tail-up animals; the Brontosaurus/Apatosaurus saga; the warm- vs cold-blooded debate), always pairing a changed idea with the evidence that changed it, and learn to judge competing interpretations by weight of evidence from multiple independent sources. The primary activity is an in-role dialogue with a scientist who lived a reversal; a theory-shift simulation, a then-vs-now comparison, and a recall-matching check are preserved as alternatives with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Interview a palaeontologist who changed their mind
feedback: If a learner says changing one's mind means the scientists were wrong or can't be trusted, reframe revision as evidence-driven improvement: ask what new evidence appeared and why the newer view is better supported.
If a learner expects one fossil to settle a question for good, discuss how strong claims rest on several independent lines of evidence agreeing, not on a single clue.
If a learner treats two scientists' disagreement as 'just opinion', surface the criterion: weigh which explanation is supported by more and better evidence from independent sources.
Reinforce when a learner pairs a changed idea with the specific evidence that changed it, rather than stating abstractly that 'science changes'.
Reinforce when a learner revises their own earlier prediction in response to the evidence offered, naming this as the same move scientists make.
activities.rationale: This META idea is about how and why minds change on evidence, so an open dialogue lets the learner interrogate the reasoning, voice their own assumptions, and hear uncertainty stated honestly. Dialogue may be well suited to conveying the human, reasoning-in-the-moment quality of revision; this is a proposed, scoped affordance that the cited sources do not establish as superior to other media, and is not a claim that other media cannot teach the idea.
sourceClaims: The scientific view of dinosaurs has been substantially revised over time — from slow, cold-blooded, scaly, tail-dragging reptiles to active, often feathered animals — as new fossil evidence (e.g. Deinonychus, feathered theropods from Liaoning) accumulated.
A core nature-of-science idea is that scientific knowledge is open to revision in light of new evidence, and scientists changing their conclusions on new evidence is a strength of the process.
learnerActions: Talk in role with a palaeontologist who began their career picturing dinosaurs as slow, scaly, tail-dragging lizards.
Before the scientist explains, make your own prediction about a disputed feature (for example, were the biggest dinosaurs feathered?), then update your prediction as evidence is presented.

Ask what changed, and have the scientist walk through concrete evidence: Deinonychus, a lightly built, sickle-clawed dinosaur whose skeleton suggested an active, agile animal rather than a sluggish one, then Liaoning fossil slabs with feathers or feather-like filaments preserved around clearly non-bird dinosaurs.

Push back with your own challenge — e.g. 'How do you KNOW those weren't just birds?' — and listen to the scientist reason it out and say honestly what is still argued (were the largest dinosaurs feathered too?).
Optionally interview a second scientist who reads a disputed fossil differently, and decide which case rests on more evidence.
State in your own words one thing scientists used to think, what they think now, and the new evidence that drove the change.
activities.intendedInsight: Good science values changing your mind when the evidence calls for it, because following the evidence — not defending old pictures — is what science is (even though some scientists resisted the new ideas at first); today's textbook is the best current answer, not the last word.

activities.title: Weigh the evidence and watch the picture shift
feedback: If a learner lets a single dramatic find flip the whole balance, point out that accepted change usually reflects accumulating evidence from multiple independent sources.
If a learner cannot say what would change their mind, prompt them to name the kind of evidence (new fossils, CT scans, bone histology) that would shift the balance.
Affirm when the learner distinguishes an evidence-rich claim from an evidence-poor one.
activities.rationale: An interactive evidence-weighing/theory-shift model may make the mechanism of revision tangible by letting the learner manipulate evidence and see the accepted picture respond. The optional balance that tips and the reconstruction that updates are concrete interaction examples, offered to make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms. It complements, rather than replaces, the dialogue's human-reasoning quality.
sourceClaims: The scientific view of dinosaurs has been substantially revised over time — from slow, cold-blooded, scaly, tail-dragging reptiles to active, often feathered animals — as new fossil evidence (e.g. Deinonychus, feathered theropods from Liaoning) accumulated.
A core nature-of-science idea is that scientific knowledge is open to revision in light of new evidence, and scientists changing their conclusions on new evidence is a strength of the process.
learnerActions: Drop newly discovered fossils onto a balance that weighs two competing hypotheses (e.g. feathered vs scaly, or warm- vs cold-blooded) and watch the 'best current picture' reconstruction update as evidence accrues.
Build a timeline of a single idea (such as dinosaur metabolism) being revised, placing each discovery where it shifted the accepted view.
Contrast an evidence-rich claim with an evidence-poor one and say which deserves more confidence and why.
Explain what new evidence would be needed to tip the balance toward the other hypothesis.
activities.intendedInsight: Revision is a reasoned mechanism: the accepted explanation moves as evidence accumulates, and the best-supported idea is the one that fits the evidence best — weighing both how much there is and how good it is — especially when several independent sources agree.

activities.title: Then-vs-now: tap to reveal what changed and why
feedback: If a learner reads the then-vs-now contrast as 'they just got it wrong', reconnect each change to the evidence that justified it.
Encourage the learner to probe further: a fixed comparison shows that an idea changed, but ask them what reasoning or competing interpretation lay behind a disputed feature.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal then-vs-now comparison can vividly show that reconstructions were revised and tie each change to its evidence. Because the display is fixed, it shows that an idea changed but cannot itself host the back-and-forth questioning needed to interrogate the reasoning or handle competing interpretations; it works best as a scaffold feeding into discussion.
sourceClaims: The scientific view of dinosaurs has been substantially revised over time — from slow, cold-blooded, scaly, tail-dragging reptiles to active, often feathered animals — as new fossil evidence (e.g. Deinonychus, feathered theropods from Liaoning) accumulated.
learnerActions: Compare an older reconstruction with today's reconstruction of the same animal (e.g. an early-1900s tail-dragging Apatosaurus/'Brontosaurus' mount, or a featherless Deinonychus from the late 1960s–70s) using paired images or a slider.
Tap individual features (posture, tail position, skin/feathers, build) to reveal what changed and the specific evidence that drove each change.
Write a sentence for one feature linking the old picture, the new picture, and the evidence between them.
activities.intendedInsight: Each visible change in how we draw dinosaurs was driven by specific evidence, often several lines of it together (such as skeletons, trackways and feather impressions) — revision is reasoned, not arbitrary.

activities.title: Match the evidence to the idea it changed
feedback: A correct match shows recall; prompt the learner to justify WHY that evidence changed that idea, so recall becomes reasoning.
If the learner frames revision as failure, revisit the dialogue or evidence-balance activity to rebuild the 'strength, not weakness' framing.
activities.rationale: A short matching check can confirm recall of which evidence drove which change. It should be used sparingly: a scored right-answer format captures recall but not the open, provisional nature of the idea, and recognition-only items do not by themselves elicit the independent reasoning the objective requires. Pair it with the open trust question above to probe understanding.
learnerActions: Match each piece of new evidence (e.g. a feathered theropod slab, a corrected skull) to the specific idea about dinosaurs it revised.
After matching, say in a sentence whether the change was driven by one clue or by several lines of evidence.
Answer the trust question in your own words: 'If scientists keep changing their minds about dinosaurs, how can we trust them at all?'
activities.intendedInsight: Recall of specific then/now changes and their driving evidence supports, but does not replace, understanding that revision is how science earns trust.

constraints: Always pair a changed idea with the specific evidence that changed it, so revision looks reasoned rather than arbitrary.
Frame mind-changing as a strength of science; counter the idea that changing conclusions means scientists were 'wrong' or unreliable.
Show competing interpretations of the same evidence to normalise disagreement that is resolved by weight of evidence from multiple independent sources.

The then-vs-now comparison and the matching check are scaffolds: being fixed/recognition-based, they confirm that ideas changed but do not by themselves elicit the learner's independent reasoning about weighing competing interpretations.
Use the matching/quiz format sparingly; a scored right-answer format risks re-freezing the misconception that science is a fixed set of correct facts.

Checkpoints differentiate: Tier A (~9) names one old vs new idea; Tier B (~10) explains what new evidence changed the picture; Tier C (~11) explains why changing one's mind is a strength and how competing ideas are judged by weight of evidence.

For this nature-of-science sequence, use dialogue, evidence weighing and then-versus-now comparisons to elicit evidence-based revision. A spatial reconstruction can be included if it helps compare evidence; no comparative effectiveness of these media is established here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources carry verified:false and have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims support the general nature-of-science principle and the historical fact of dinosaur reconstruction revision; they do NOT establish comparative efficacy of dialogue over simulation/image, nor that any specific activity here was tested. Fit rankings in the original ('ideal', 'strong', 'poor') were catalog preferences and were not treated as evidence.

The original asserted that a simulation or picture 'cannot' capture the human reasoning quality and that a static image 'can't' let a child probe reasoning; these were softened to scoped, proposed affordances/limits, since the sources do not establish such necessity claims.

Specific fossil/method details (Deinonychus, Liaoning feathered theropods, CT scans, bone histology, Brontosaurus/Apatosaurus) are drawn from the source row and pedagogy notes and were not independently re-verified in this rewrite.

probeDeeper: Give an example of a dinosaur idea that changed — what NEW evidence caused the change?
Two scientists look at the SAME fossil and disagree — how could you decide who has the stronger case?
Is it a weakness or a strength of science that it can change its mind? Why?
What would make you trust one explanation of a fossil more than another?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning treats changing ideas as a STRENGTH, not a failure: scientific knowledge updates as new fossils and new methods (feather fossils, CT scans, bone histology) give better evidence. The same fossil can be interpreted differently, so the explanation to trust is the one backed by the most evidence from several independent sources. Trust comes from evidence and self-correction, not from never changing one's mind.

errorPatterns.pattern: If scientists change their minds they were wrong before, so they can't be trusted.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe revision as evidence-driven improvement — ask what new evidence appeared and why the newer view is better supported.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats any revision as proof of unreliability; expects science to be fixed, certain facts.

errorPatterns.pattern: One big discovery or clue settles a scientific question for good.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss how strong claims rest on multiple independent lines of evidence agreeing, not on one clue.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects a single fossil to prove a theory outright.

errorPatterns.pattern: When two scientists disagree it's just opinion — there's no way to choose.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Surface the criterion — weigh which explanation is supported by more and better evidence from independent sources.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats competing explanations as equally valid matters of opinion.

responseLevels.gap: Treats changing ideas as proof science is unreliable, or science as a fixed set of facts, with no notion of evidence driving change.
responseLevels.full: Frames revision as evidence-driven self-correction, gives a concrete example of changed dinosaur knowledge, and argues the best explanation is the one supported by the most evidence from multiple independent sources — engaging thoughtfully with the trust question.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts that ideas change with new evidence and can give an example, but can't articulate HOW to weigh competing interpretations (multiple independent lines of evidence).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Scientists once pictured dinosaurs as sluggish, scaly, cold-blooded reptiles; now many are shown as active, feathered, and possibly warm-blooded. Some people say, 'If scientists keep changing their minds about dinosaurs, how can we trust them at all?' How would you answer that?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: It separates a child who reads any revision as science 'failing' or being untrustworthy from one who sees revision-in-light-of-evidence as how science earns trust and weighs competing interpretations.
